items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Hydrologists studying forested watersheds in Oregon found that removing streamside trees raised summer water temperatures in narrow headwater creeks by several degrees. Along wide rivers, however, the same kind of clearing produced no measurable warming. The researchers explained that a wide river's surface is mostly exposed to the sun even when its banks are forested, so the trees provide little shade to begin with. If a timber project cleared the trees along both a narrow headwater creek and a wide river, the clearing would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: raise the water temperature of the headwater creek but not that of the wide river.
raise the water temperature of the wide river but not that of the headwater creek.
lower the water temperature of the headwater creek but not that of the wide river.
raise the water temperatures of the creek and the river by roughly equal amounts.
items.explanation: Write the finding as one arrow: clearing streamside trees → warmer water → narrow creeks only. Apply it to the new project and you get warming in the creek and no change in the wide river. That is choice A.

B.why: You got the direction right (warming) but swapped the groups. The passage says the wide river showed no measurable warming, and the narrow creek is the one that warmed.

C.why: You got the group right (the creek) but reversed the direction. Taking away shade makes the creek warmer, not cooler.

D.why: You let the effect spread to both water bodies. The passage says clearing had no measurable effect on wide rivers, so equal warming is not supported.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: When a regional insurance company began letting employees work from home three days a week, economist Dana Whitcomb tracked how many workers quit over the next two years. Among employees with commutes longer than an hour, the share who quit fell sharply. Among employees who lived within a short drive of the office, the share who quit hardly changed. Whitcomb's findings suggest that if the company were to end its remote-work policy, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: employees who live close to the office would likely become more likely to quit.
employees with long commutes would likely become less likely to quit.
employees with long commutes would likely become more likely to quit.
employees across the company would likely quit at much higher rates.
items.explanation: The arrow is: remote work → fewer quits → long-commute employees only. Ending the policy runs that arrow backward, so quitting should rise among long-commute employees. That is choice C.

A.why: You got the direction right but picked the wrong group. Quit rates for nearby employees hardly changed when the policy started, so you have no reason to expect them to change when it ends.

B.why: You got the group right but kept the original direction. The policy reduced quitting, so taking it away would raise quitting, not lower it.

D.why: You applied the effect to everyone and made it bigger. The study found an effect only among long-commute employees, so a company-wide jump goes beyond the evidence.

items.stimulus: Archaeologists compared wooden tools buried in two kinds of soil at the same site. Tools in dry, sandy soil, where air moves freely, had mostly rotted away. Tools in waterlogged clay, which holds very little oxygen, were nearly intact. The team concluded that oxygen is what drives the decay. Based on this finding, draining the clay so that air could reach it would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: slow the decay of the tools buried in the clay.
speed the decay of the tools buried in the clay.
speed the decay of the tools buried in the sand.
speed the decay of every tool buried at the site.
items.explanation: Write the finding as one arrow: more oxygen → faster decay. Clay tools survived because the clay held little oxygen. Draining the clay lets air in, so oxygen goes up for the clay tools, and their decay should speed up. Both the direction (speed) and the group (clay) have to be right. This is the basic move behind every 'apply the finding to a new case' inference question: write the arrow first, then push the change through it.

A.why: You picked the right group but flipped the direction. Draining adds oxygen, and the passage says oxygen drives decay, so decay speeds up. It does not slow down.

D.why: You stretched one group's change to everything. Draining the clay changes conditions only in the clay. The sand tools' situation stays the same.

A comparison of forty small catchments by hydrologist Ines Halvorsen complicates that view. During short, intense downpours, peak streamflow in heavily paved catchments was far higher than in unpaved ones. During long, soaking storms, however, unpaved soil quickly became saturated and shed water almost as fast as pavement did, so peak flows in the two kinds of catchment were nearly identical. If a region's climate shifted toward fewer short downpours and more prolonged rainfall, the difference in flood peaks between its paved and unpaved catchments would therefore ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: likely shrink, since more of its storms would be the kind in which paving makes little difference to peak flow.
likely grow, since prolonged rainfall would send more total water off paved catchments than off unpaved ones.
likely shrink, since paved surfaces would begin absorbing rainfall nearly as well as saturated soil does.
likely grow, since short downpours are the storms in which paving most increases peak streamflow.
items.explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: short, intense storms → much higher peaks in paved catchments; long storms → almost no difference. The change in the question is fewer short storms and more long ones. That moves more of the region's storms into the 'almost no difference' category, so the gap between paved and unpaved catchments should shrink. Choice A gets both the direction and the reason right.

B.why: You brought in an idea the passage never states, that total runoff volume decides the gap. The study measured peak flow, and during long storms those peaks were nearly identical. More long storms means a smaller gap, not a bigger one.

C.why: You got the direction right but credited the change to the wrong surface. In the passage, the soil changes: it saturates and starts behaving like pavement. Nothing says pavement starts behaving like soil.

D.why: You remembered the right mechanism, that paving matters most in short downpours, but ran it backward. The question says those downpours become less common, so paving's effect shows up less often, which shrinks the gap instead of growing it.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: When the city of Marrow Falls required employers to offer paid sick leave, economists expected employee turnover to drop across the whole workforce. Labor economist Dario Okafor found a narrower effect. Turnover fell sharply among part-time hourly workers, most of whom had had no paid leave before the mandate. Among full-time salaried workers, nearly all of whom already received paid leave from their employers, turnover did not change measurably. Suppose a neighboring city with an almost entirely full-time salaried workforce, already widely covered by employer leave policies, adopted the same mandate. That city would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: see little change in overall turnover, since the mandate mainly affected workers who had previously lacked paid leave.
see a sharp drop in turnover among its salaried workers, since the mandate sharply reduced turnover in Marrow Falls.
see turnover rise among its few part-time workers, since mandated leave makes those positions costlier to offer.
see a sharp drop in overall turnover, since the mandate's effect did not depend on which workers it reached.
items.explanation: The arrow is: mandate → lower turnover → only for workers who had no leave before. Already-covered salaried workers showed no change. The new city's workforce is almost entirely made up of that unaffected group, so the mandate should leave overall turnover there nearly unchanged.

B.why: You kept the direction, a drop in turnover, but attached it to the wrong group. In Marrow Falls, the sharp drop happened among part-time hourly workers. Salaried workers showed no measurable change.

C.why: You turned the direction around by adding a cost argument the passage never makes. The only evidence about part-time workers shows their turnover fell under the mandate.

D.why: The passage's main point is that the effect did depend on which workers the mandate reached. Assuming a uniform drop brings back the popular expectation that the study undercut.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Ornithologist Priya Venkataraman recorded marsh sparrows nesting near wind turbines, which emit a steady low-frequency hum. Males whose songs were naturally low-pitched raised the lowest notes of their songs, apparently so that the hum would not drown them out. Males whose songs were naturally high-pitched, and therefore already above the hum's range, did not change their songs. Venkataraman concluded that the shift was a direct response to the masking noise. If the turbines were replaced with models producing much less low-frequency hum, then ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: males with low-pitched songs would likely lower their lowest notes, while high-pitched singers would change little.
males with high-pitched songs would likely lower their lowest notes, while low-pitched singers would change little.
males with low-pitched songs would likely raise their lowest notes, while high-pitched singers would change little.
males with either low- or high-pitched songs would likely lower their lowest notes by roughly equal amounts.
items.explanation: The arrow is: low-frequency hum → raised lowest notes → only in naturally low-pitched singers. If you remove most of the hum, the pressure that raised those notes goes away, so the low-pitched singers should drift back down. High-pitched singers never responded to the hum, so they should stay about the same.

B.why: You got the direction right but swapped the groups. The high-pitched singers never changed their songs, so there is nothing for them to undo. The low-pitched singers are the ones who shifted.

C.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Raising notes was the response to the hum. With the hum mostly gone, those birds have reason to come back down, not to rise further.

D.why: You applied the finding to every male even though the passage says only low-pitched singers responded to the noise. Nothing supports an equal change among high-pitched singers.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: It is often assumed that older adults gain the most from vaccine boosters simply because of their age. Immunologist Tomasz Reyes found otherwise. A booster sharply raised antibody levels in participants over 65 whose levels had waned substantially since their first dose, but older participants whose levels had stayed high gained only as modestly as younger participants did. The size of the gain tracked how far antibody levels had fallen before the booster, not the recipient's age. If older adults received the booster much sooner after their first dose, before much waning had occurred, their gain in antibody levels would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: be smaller than in the study, because their antibody levels would still be close to where they started.
be larger than in the study, because older adults respond more strongly to boosters than younger adults do.
be smaller than in the study, because younger adults would then gain more from the booster than older adults.
be larger than in the study, because an earlier booster leaves antibodies more time to keep accumulating.
items.explanation: The arrow is: more waning before the booster → bigger gain, regardless of age. Giving the booster earlier means less waning, so older adults would start from higher levels and see a smaller gain, just like the older participants whose levels had stayed high.

B.why: You went back to the popular view that the passage rejects. Reyes found that the gain depended on how much antibody levels had waned, not on age, so age alone can't produce a larger boost.

C.why: You got the direction right but moved the reasoning to a different group. The question asks about older adults' own gain compared with the study. How younger adults compare is beside the point and isn't established anyway.

D.why: You flipped the direction by adding a mechanism the passage never mentions. According to the study, an earlier booster means less waning, and less waning means a smaller gain.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Astronomers often estimate how quickly a galaxy forms stars by measuring its ultraviolet light, which young, massive stars emit in abundance. Interstellar dust, however, absorbs ultraviolet light, so in dusty galaxies much of that light never reaches telescopes, while in nearly dust-free galaxies almost all of it does. Radio emission linked to the same young stars passes through dust almost unimpeded. If a survey replaced its ultraviolet-based estimates with radio-based ones, the star formation rates it reports for the dustiest galaxies would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: rise substantially, while the rates it reports for nearly dust-free galaxies would change little.
fall substantially, while the rates it reports for nearly dust-free galaxies would change little.
change little, while the rates it reports for nearly dust-free galaxies would rise substantially.
rise substantially, and the rates it reports for nearly dust-free galaxies would rise by as much.
items.explanation: The arrow is: dust → lost ultraviolet light → star formation underestimated, mainly in dusty galaxies. Radio emission avoids that loss, so switching to it should push the dusty galaxies' estimates up. Dust-free galaxies lost almost no light to begin with, so their estimates should barely change.

B.why: You picked the right group but the wrong direction. Dust hides ultraviolet light, so the old estimates for dusty galaxies were too low. Correcting them raises them.

C.why: You swapped the groups. Dust-free galaxies already delivered almost all their ultraviolet light, so their estimates were accurate. The dusty galaxies are the ones whose numbers would jump.

D.why: You stretched the correction to every galaxy. The passage says almost all ultraviolet light from dust-free galaxies reaches telescopes, so there is little for the switch to correct there.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Many cartographers assume that hillshading, the simulated shadows that make terrain look three-dimensional on a flat map, helps every reader understand the land. In a 2023 study, however, geographer Ilse Marten found that its benefit is narrower. Novice map readers given hillshaded maps chose correct hiking routes far more often than novices given otherwise identical unshaded maps. Experienced orienteers, by contrast, performed equally well with either version. Marten's findings suggest that if a park agency removed hillshading from its trail maps to cut printing costs, doing so would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: reduce route-finding accuracy among novice hikers while leaving experienced hikers' accuracy largely unchanged.
reduce route-finding accuracy among experienced hikers while leaving novice hikers' accuracy largely unchanged.
improve route-finding accuracy among novice hikers while leaving experienced hikers' accuracy largely unchanged.
reduce route-finding accuracy among novice and experienced hikers by roughly the same amount.
items.explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: hillshading → better route choices → novices only. Experienced orienteers did equally well with or without it. Removing hillshading reverses the condition, so the novices' advantage should disappear and their accuracy should fall. Experienced hikers never depended on the shading, so their accuracy should stay about the same. Only A gets both the direction (reduce) and the group (novices) right.

B.why: You got the direction right but swapped the groups. The passage says experienced orienteers performed equally well with or without hillshading, so removing it should not hurt them. It is the novices who relied on it.

C.why: You picked the right group but reversed the direction. Hillshading helped novices, so taking it away should lower their accuracy, not raise it.

D.why: This is the popular view the passage sets up to knock down: that hillshading helps everyone. Marten found that experienced orienteers were unaffected, so you have no grounds to expect an equal loss in both groups.

items.stimulus: When one state required employers to provide paid sick leave, economist Rafael Okonjo tracked how often workers left their jobs. Turnover among part-time workers fell sharply after the mandate took effect, while turnover among full-time workers stayed essentially flat. Okonjo attributes this split to a single factor: before the law, most full-time workers in the state already received paid sick leave, but few part-time workers did. If Okonjo is correct, a similar mandate adopted in a state where few full-time workers currently receive paid sick leave would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: reduce turnover among part-time workers but not among full-time workers.
reduce turnover among full-time workers as well as among part-time workers.
raise turnover among full-time workers while reducing it among part-time workers.
reduce turnover among full-time workers but not among part-time workers.
items.explanation: Write Okonjo's explanation as an arrow: newly gaining paid leave → lower turnover. Full-time workers in the first state showed no change only because they already had leave. In the new state, few full-time workers have leave, so they would be newly covered just as the part-time workers were. Both groups should therefore see turnover fall.

A.why: You copied the first state's result without applying the reason behind it. The full-time group was unaffected only because it was already covered. In the new state it isn't covered, so the explanation predicts that full-time workers would benefit too.

C.why: You reversed the direction for full-time workers. Nothing in the passage suggests that gaining paid leave makes anyone more likely to quit. The mechanism runs toward lower turnover.

D.why: You dropped the part-time group. Part-time workers lack paid leave in the new state as well, so by Okonjo's reasoning their turnover should also fall.

items.stimulus: Dietary guidelines often present high-fiber diets as a reliable way to lower blood sugar. Nutrition scientist Hana Kovač found that the effect depends on the gut. lower fasting glucose among patients lacking Prevotella but not among patients whose gut bacteria include it.
raise fasting glucose among patients whose gut bacteria include Prevotella but not among patients lacking it.
lower fasting glucose among all patients, though more among those whose gut bacteria include Prevotella.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Radiocarbon dating measures when a plant or animal stopped absorbing carbon from the atmosphere. Charcoal from long-lived trees therefore poses a problem: a beam of oak may contain inner rings that formed centuries before the tree was felled and burned, so it can yield a date far older than the fire itself. Short-lived materials such as charred seeds avoid this flaw, because they formed within a year of being burned. A hearth that was first dated to 1200 BCE using oak charcoal, if redated using seeds from the same hearth, would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: yield a date later than 1200 BCE, indicating that the hearth was used more recently than first thought.
yield a date earlier than 1200 BCE, indicating that the hearth was used longer ago than first thought.
yield a date close to 1200 BCE, since seeds and charcoal both record when the hearth was in use.
yield a date later than 1200 BCE, indicating that the oak was felled more recently than first thought.
items.explanation: Write the flaw as an arrow: oak charcoal → date too old → for the fire. Seeds fix that flaw, so a seed date should be younger, meaning a later calendar date than 1200 BCE. That later date tells you about the fire, and so about when people used the hearth. Only A gets both the direction (later) and the thing being dated (the hearth's use) right.

B.why: You reversed the direction. The passage says oak charcoal makes dates too old, so correcting the error moves the date forward in time, not further back.

C.why: This ignores the flaw the passage spells out. Charcoal from old wood does not reliably record when the fire burned, which is exactly why seeds are described as the better material.

D.why: You got the direction right but attached it to the wrong thing. Seeds formed in the year of the fire, so they date the hearth's use. They say nothing about when the oak was cut.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Amateur astronomers in brightly lit cities often attach "nebula filters" to their telescopes, believing the filters improve views of every faint object. A survey led by astronomer Dalia Ferro found otherwise. The filters, which pass only the few wavelengths given off by glowing gas, made emission nebulae markedly easier to detect. They made galaxies, whose starlight spans a broad range of wavelengths, harder to detect. Ferro's results suggest that an observer who removed such a filter would likely find ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: galaxies easier to detect and emission nebulae harder to detect.
emission nebulae easier to detect and galaxies harder to detect.
both galaxies and emission nebulae harder to detect than before.
galaxies easier to detect and emission nebulae no harder to detect.
items.explanation: Write the finding as two arrows. With the filter on: nebulae → easier to detect, galaxies → harder to detect. Removing the filter reverses both arrows, so galaxies should become easier to detect and nebulae harder. Only A flips both directions and keeps each one with the right kind of object.

B.why: This describes what the filter does when it's on, not what happens when it's removed. You read the finding correctly but didn't reverse it for the change the question names.

C.why: This follows the popular belief that the filter helps with every faint object, so taking it off must make everything worse. Ferro found that the filter actually hurt galaxy views, so removing it should help with galaxies.

D.why: You got the galaxies right but missed the nebulae. The filter made nebulae markedly easier to detect, so taking it away should make them harder to detect.

The study's findings suggest that if the city repealed the tax, ______

purchases in low-income households would likely rise, while those in high-income households would change little.

items.stimulus: Historians long assumed that the flying shuttle, introduced to English looms in 1733, sped up all hand weaving about equally. gained less from the device than broadcloth workshops did.
produced roughly as much cloth each day as before.
used a device once thought to speed all weaving.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Economists studying a city's 2019 paid-sick-leave mandate found that it reduced quitting among hourly restaurant workers by about 20 percent. Turnover among salaried restaurant managers, nearly all of whom already received paid leave from their employers before the law, did not change. hourly workers to start quitting more often than before.
managers' turnover to stay close to its earlier level.
hourly turnover to shift more than managers' turnover.

D.why: This is the swapped-group trap. The hourly group is the one the law affected, so repeal should change hourly turnover more than managers' turnover. If you mixed up which group the law affected, you'd think this was unexpected.

items.stimulus: Many planners assume that restored wetlands guard against flooding in every storm. help in a smaller share of the basin's storms.
continue to cut peak flows in moderate storms.
matter least in storms falling on saturated soil.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Many planners assume that converting curbside parking into protected bike lanes reduces driving across an entire district. A study of the Eastgate district of Halvorsen complicates that view. After a lane opened, residents living within 500 meters of it made fewer car trips shorter than 3 kilometers, while their car trips longer than 3 kilometers held steady. Residents living farther away showed no change in either kind of trip. These results suggest that if the city extended the lane so that a neighborhood now 2 kilometers away fell within 500 meters of it, that neighborhood's residents would likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: make fewer car trips both shorter and longer than 3 kilometers than they did before the extension.
make about as many car trips of every length as before, as the study's more distant residents did.
make fewer car trips shorter than 3 kilometers while making about as many longer car trips as before.
make about as many car trips shorter than 3 kilometers while making fewer longer car trips than before.
items.explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: living within 500 meters of the lane leads to fewer short car trips (under 3 kilometers) and no change in long ones. Living farther away leads to no change at all. The extension moves the neighborhood from the far group into the near group, so its residents should now follow the near-group pattern. That means fewer short trips and steady long trips. You have to carry both halves of the near-group result forward, not just the fact that the neighborhood is now close.

D.why: You got the group right but swapped the trip lengths. In the study, short car trips fell and long ones held steady. This choice reverses that, which is the mirror-image trap this question type is built around.

items.stimulus: Mycorrhizal fungi colonize crop roots and extend them into the surrounding soil, and some seed suppliers market fungal inoculants as a general boost to yield. items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Cartographers have long assumed that printing more contour lines makes a topographic map easier to read. Psychologist Lena Okafor's work complicates that assumption. In her study, hikers judged the steepness of slopes shown on maps. Experienced hikers' estimates tracked the contour interval printed in each map's legend, but novices' estimates tracked only how tightly the lines were packed, whatever the interval. Okafor's findings therefore suggest that if a park reissued its trail maps with the contour interval reduced from 20 meters to 10 meters, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: novice hikers would likely judge the park's slopes to be steeper than before, while experienced hikers' judgments would change little.
experienced hikers would likely judge the park's slopes to be steeper than before, while novice hikers' judgments would change little.
novice hikers would likely judge the park's slopes to be less steep than before, while experienced hikers' judgments would change little.
novice and experienced hikers alike would likely judge the park's slopes to be steeper than before, since both would see more lines.
items.explanation: Write the finding as an arrow: tighter line packing → judged steeper → novices only. Halving the interval puts twice as many lines on the same terrain, so the lines sit closer together. Novices read that packing as steepness, so they judge the slopes steeper. Experienced hikers read the legend, notice the new interval and correct for it, so their judgments barely move.

C.why: You picked the right group but reversed the direction, probably because a smaller interval sounds like a more precise map. More precision doesn't help the novices, who ignore the interval. They only see lines packed closer, and that reads as steeper.

D.why: You applied the change to everyone. The passage says experienced hikers' estimates followed the legend, so they would adjust for the new interval rather than be misled by the extra lines.

items.stimulus: Astronomers often describe light pollution as a threat to all ground-based observing. Analyzing ten years of records from a hilltop telescope, Mei Tanaka found a narrower effect: on nights when the glow from a nearby town brightened the sky, the telescope recorded markedly fewer faint galaxies than usual, whereas its counts of bright galaxies did not change. Tanaka's analysis suggests that if the town replaced its streetlights with fixtures that send less light skyward, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the telescope's counts of bright galaxies would likely rise, while its counts of faint galaxies would hold steady.
the telescope's counts of faint galaxies would likely fall, while its counts of bright galaxies would hold steady.
the telescope's counts of faint and bright galaxies would both likely rise, since the sky would be darker overall.
the telescope's counts of faint galaxies would likely rise, while its counts of bright galaxies would hold steady.
items.explanation: The arrow is: brighter sky → fewer galaxies recorded → faint galaxies only. The new streetlights make the sky darker, which reverses the condition, so the effect reverses too: faint-galaxy counts should rise. Bright-galaxy counts weren't affected by sky glow in the first place, so they should stay the same.

A.why: You got the direction right but swapped the groups. Bright-galaxy counts stayed the same even on bright nights, so a darker sky has nothing to restore for them.

B.why: You picked the right group but kept the original direction. Fewer counts went with a brighter sky. This change makes the sky darker, so faint-galaxy counts should go up.

C.why: You went back to the popular view that the passage opens with and then corrects. Tanaka found that sky glow affected only faint galaxies, so darkening the sky shouldn't change the bright counts.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Paving over land is usually blamed for worsening every flood downstream. Hydrologist Ruth Abernathy's records from a suburban river complicate that view. After its watershed was largely paved, peak flows from modest storms nearly doubled, but peak flows from the largest storms barely changed, because in those storms even unpaved soil quickly became saturated and shed water as fast as pavement did. Abernathy's data suggest that if the watershed's parking lots were rebuilt with porous paving that lets rain soak into the ground, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: peak flows from the largest storms would likely fall, while those from modest storms would change little.
peak flows from modest storms would likely fall, while those from the largest storms would change little.
peak flows from modest storms would likely rise, while those from the largest storms would change little.
peak flows from storms of every size would likely fall, by roughly the same proportion in each case.
items.explanation: The arrow is: paving → higher peak flows → modest storms only, because in the largest storms soaked soil sheds water as fast as pavement does. Porous paving lets rain soak in, which partly undoes the paving, so modest-storm peaks should come down. In the largest storms the ground under porous paving also fills up quickly, so those peaks should change little.

A.why: You got the direction right but gave it to the wrong storms, probably because the largest floods seem to matter most. The passage says paving barely affected the largest storms, so undoing it won't change them much either.

C.why: You picked the right storms but reversed the direction. Porous paving lets water soak in, which works against the paving effect. It lowers peak flows.

D.why: You went back to the 'every flood' view that the passage corrects. Abernathy's records show the largest storms responding differently, and the passage explains why.

items.subtype_name: Apply the finding one step forward
items.stimulus: Many clinics schedule vaccinations whenever it is convenient, on the assumption that timing is irrelevant. Immunologist Kwame Asante's trial suggests otherwise for some patients: adults over 65 who received an influenza vaccine in the morning developed substantially higher antibody levels than those vaccinated in the afternoon, whereas among adults under 40, timing made no measurable difference. If a clinic serving a retirement community and a clinic serving university students both moved their vaccinations from mornings to afternoons, Asante's findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: antibody levels would likely fall more among the students than among the retirement community's residents.
antibody levels would likely rise more among the retirement community's residents than among the students.
antibody levels would likely fall more among the retirement community's residents than among the students.
antibody levels would likely fall by about the same amount among both the residents and the students.
items.explanation: The arrow is: morning vaccination → higher antibodies → only adults over 65. Here the clinics move from morning to afternoon, the less favorable time, so the effect runs downward. The retirement community's residents are the older group, so their antibody levels would drop. The students are under 40, so timing doesn't affect them and their levels hold.

A.why: You got the direction right but gave it to the wrong group. Timing made no measurable difference for adults under 40, which is the students' group.

B.why: You picked the right group but took the direction from the finding rather than from the change. The finding favors mornings, and these clinics are giving up mornings, so older patients' antibody levels go down.

D.why: You applied the effect to everyone. The passage gives the timing effect only to older adults and specifically rules it out for younger ones.
